title: What isn't done, and why (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2)
hookLine: thirty-nine kinds of creative work, linked to building the tabernacle, are set aside

cards: You can carry a heavy table across the living room, and on Shabbat it's fine. But in many observant homes, you won't flip a light switch, or write a two-letter word on a sticky note. That sounds backward.
Moving furniture is hard; writing is easy. If Shabbat is about rest, why is the easy thing off the table? Because the Hebrew word usually translated as work doesn't mean effort at all.

teach.b: Melacha means creative work: the kind that makes something, changes the world, or puts your stamp on it. The Torah says don't do melacha on Shabbat, but it barely says what melacha is.
One example it does give, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." So how did the rabbis define it?
Right after that verse, the Torah turns to building the mishkan, the tabernacle that closed camp two.

teach.h: SIDE BY SIDE WITH THE MISHKAN.
teach.b: Shabbat and the mishkan, side by side. So the rabbis said: whatever kinds of work it took to build the mishkan, those are the kinds you set aside on Shabbat. Six days a week, you can build a holy place in space.
On the seventh, you stop, and live in holy time.
The Mishnah lists them: forty less one, thirty-nine. They read like a tour of a workshop in the ancient world. Sowing, plowing, reaping, grinding, kneading, baking.
Shearing, dyeing, spinning, weaving, sewing. Writing two letters, erasing. Building, tearing down.

Kindling a fire, putting one out. Carrying from one domain to another. Later rabbis' rulings about modern life, from cars to electricity, grow out of those thirty-nine, and Jewish movements apply them differently.
Orthodox Jews keep them in detail.
Other Jews keep some, or choose their own ways to rest.
The idea underneath is the same, and it's a surprising one: for one day, you stop being the one who shapes the world, and let the world be.

how: Observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of melacha from sundown Friday until Saturday night, preparing food, lights and other needs in advance; other Jews keep some of them or set aside work in their own ways.

o: a paid job done for an employer
any task that makes you tired or sweaty
creative work that makes or changes things

p: the work that defines the list

melacha means creative work; carrying a table inside the house can be fine while writing is not.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis. the Torah says no melacha on Shabbat but barely says what it is. where do you look for a definition?
o: the work of building the mishkan.
games.why: the Torah puts Shabbat right beside the building of the mishkan, so the rabbis defined melacha by the work that built it: thirty-nine kinds.

practice: Run through your day in your mind and notice the ways you make and change things: typing, buying, cooking, fixing, editing, posting.
Pick one, small, not because it's hard but because it's yours, and picture a few hours this week set aside from it: your hands still, the world going on without your edits.

wordCard.voice: Melacha. Creative work, not effort: thirty-nine kinds, drawn from building the mishkan, set aside on Shabbat.

orig.note: Hebrew: creative work, craft. often linked to malach, a messenger, one sent to do a task.

carryVoice: Your line: not doing is a practice. Thirty-nine kinds of making, set down for a day. See you tomorrow.
